Public Adjuster Intake Process: The First 10 Minutes

# Public Adjuster Intake Process: The First Ten Minutes After a Lead

 by aberrantmarketing | Sep 29, 2026 | Blog

The public adjuster intake process is the ten minutes between a property owner reaching out and a licensed adjuster owning the file, and it is where most marketing money is either converted or quietly thrown away. Every dollar spent on SEO, ads, and reviews exists to produce that first contact. What happens next is not a marketing problem. It is an operations problem, and almost nobody in this industry has designed it on purpose.

### Public Adjuster Intake Process: Key Points

- Speed decides intake: a widely cited lead response study found the odds of qualifying a lead fall off sharply after the first five minutes, and most firms take hours.
- The person who answers can gather facts, show empathy, and book the inspection. If they are unlicensed, they cannot advise on the claim, the coverage, or the value.
- A missed call is not a lost lead until it goes unanswered for a day. A text inside five minutes and an email that says what to gather keeps the file alive.
- Every call should carry its source with it, so the firm knows which page, ad, or referral produced the signing, not just the ring.

## Why the Public Adjuster Intake Process Decides What Your Marketing Was Worth

Ask a firm owner how many leads came in last month and you will usually get a number. Ask how many of those leads were spoken to within ten minutes, by whom, and what was said, and the room goes quiet. That gap is the intake process, and it is the single largest variable in marketing ROI for a public adjusting firm that nobody puts on the dashboard.

Here is why it matters more for public adjusters than for almost any other business. A property owner who reaches out is usually at the worst moment of the year. They have a denied or lowballed claim, a contractor in the driveway, and a carrier adjuster who has already given them a number. They are calling three firms, not one, and the firm that picks up, sounds calm, and gets an inspection on the calendar is the firm that signs the file. Everyone else gets a voicemail they will never listen to.

We see this from the marketing side every week. Two firms in the same city, similar websites, similar ad spend, and one signs twice as many claims. The difference is never the landing page. It is who answered, how fast, and whether the call ended with a date. If you have read our guide to public adjuster lead generation, you already know we measure signed claims rather than lead counts. Intake is where the two numbers separate.

## Minute Zero: Who Picks Up, and What the Law Lets Them Say

Minute zero is the ring. Before a word is spoken, the firm has already made its most important intake decision: who answers. There are three options, and each has a cost. A licensed adjuster answers personally, which converts best and scales worst. A trained intake person answers, which scales well and needs a script and a hard boundary. Or nobody answers, and the phone goes to voicemail, which is the option most firms have chosen without meaning to.

### Facts, Empathy, and the Next Step. Nothing About the Claim.

The first thirty seconds of a good intake call do three things in order. They confirm the basics: name, property address, what happened and when, and where the claim stands with the carrier. They acknowledge the situation in plain words, because the caller is stressed and the calm voice on the line is doing half the selling. And they set the next step, which is an inspection by a licensed adjuster, not an opinion over the phone.

What the first thirty seconds do not do is evaluate the claim. Nobody on a first call should say the carrier's number is wrong, that the roof is a total loss, or that the policy covers the loss. Those are judgments only a licensed adjuster makes, after an inspection, and saying them early creates two problems: a promise the file may not keep, and a compliance exposure the firm does not need.

### The Unlicensed Staff Line Most Firms Have Never Drawn

The NAIC Public Adjuster Licensing Model Act, which most state statutes are built on, bars a public adjuster from letting unlicensed employees perform licensed activity. Advising a policyholder on their claim is licensed activity. Gathering facts, expressing sympathy, explaining that the firm inspects before it advises, and booking that inspection are not. That is the line, and every intake script should be written on the safe side of it.

In practice the line is simple to hold. An unlicensed intake person says what the firm does, asks what happened, and books the licensed adjuster. They do not say whether the caller has a case, what it is worth, or what the carrier did wrong. If the caller pushes, the answer is a good one: the adjuster will look at the property and the policy and tell you plainly, which is worth more than a guess on the phone. State law controls, and this is education rather than legal advice.

### You Built the Firm to Fight for Policyholders, Not to Sit by the Phone

We understand why intake slips. You are on a roof, in a mediation, or on the phone with a carrier when the next lead calls. We bring the tracking, the script structure, and the follow-up sequence so the firm answers well even when you cannot.

## Minutes One Through Five: The Questions That Qualify Without Advising

Once the basics are down, the next four minutes decide whether this is a file the firm wants and whether the caller wants the firm. Qualification is not interrogation. It is a short set of questions that any intake person can ask without crossing into advice, and the answers tell a licensed adjuster everything they need before the inspection.

### What to Ask on Every First Call

- What happened, and roughly when? A date, even an approximate one, is the first thing the adjuster will need.
- Has a claim been filed with the carrier, and where does it stand: unreported, filed, inspected, offered, or denied?
- Has anyone else looked at the damage: a contractor, a roofer, a carrier adjuster, an engineer?
- Is the property residential or commercial, owner occupied or rented, and is anyone living in it right now?
- How did you find us? Ask it every time, because it is the one question that ties the marketing spend to the signature.

### What Never Gets Said on a First Call

Three things are off the table on a first call, no matter who is answering. The firm does not tell the caller they have damage that has not been inspected. The firm does not say what the claim is worth or promise a result. And the firm does not present itself as anything other than a public adjuster working for the policyholder, which means no blurring the line with the carrier's adjuster and no running down a carrier by name.

These are not just good manners. Each one maps to a provision in the Model Act and in the public adjuster advertising rules that vary by state. A firm that trains its intake staff on those three lines has removed most of its phone-call risk in one afternoon.

## Minutes Five Through Ten: Booking the Inspection Before the Call Ends

The only good way to end a first call is with a date. A property owner who hangs up with a promise that someone will call back is a property owner who will sign with whichever firm calls first, and it is rarely the one that promised. A property owner who hangs up with an inspection on Thursday at two has stopped shopping.

That means the intake person needs the licensed adjuster's calendar in front of them, the authority to book it, and a plain explanation of what the inspection is: a licensed adjuster walks the property and reads the policy, then tells the owner plainly where they stand. Nothing is signed on the phone. The contract, the disclosure the state requires, and the owner's right to cancel are handled in person, by the person licensed to handle them.
